Posterior density of a diagnostic

Source: R/accessors.R
functional_density.Rd

Computes the exact posterior density of a diagnostic or of the between-site standard deviation on a grid of values.

Usage

functional_density(
  x,
  which = c("I", "mean", "H", "J_eff", "sigma_tau"),
  n = 512
)

Arguments

x

An object of class reliability_posterior.

which

The quantity: one of "I" (the default), "mean", "H", "J_eff" or "sigma_tau".

n

Number of points of the grid, an integer of at least 10.

Value

A data frame with the columns value and density.

Details

The density follows from that of sigma_tau by a change of variables: for an increasing quantity \(f\), the density at \(f(\sigma)\) is \(g(\sigma) / f'(\sigma)\). For the dispersion \(H\) the terms of the two branches on either side of its largest value are added, with \(dH/d\sigma = 2(\bar S - I)/\sigma\). Under every prior of sd_prior() the posterior density of sigma_tau has a finite positive limit at 0. The densities of \(I\) and the mean reliability grow without bound at their values for sigma_tau = 0, like the inverse square root of the distance from that value; they are still integrable. This behavior also applies to \(H\) and the concentration count when the standard errors are unequal. With equal standard errors, their posteriors are point masses at 0 and \(J\), respectively.

The grid spans the central 99.9% of the posterior, so a plot of the density does not include the extreme tails. With equal sampling variances, \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) is a point mass at \(J\), has no density, and asking for one is an error. When the sampling variances differ so little (by about 1e-6 relative or less) that the derivative of \(J_{\mathrm{eff}}\) cannot be computed reliably, asking for its density is an error too.

Examples

fit <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = eight_schools)
head(functional_density(fit, "I", n = 50))
#>          value     density
#> 1 1.599263e-07 1563.220044
#> 2 1.913529e-02    4.543663
#> 3 3.827043e-02    3.226804
#> 4 5.740556e-02    2.643285
#> 5 7.654069e-02    2.294170
#> 6 9.567583e-02    2.054244
